newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU says still ready to sell wheat despite slowdown.
newsitem.headline: EU says still ready to sell wheat despite slowdown.

text.p: A top European Union farm official sought on Tuesday to reassure grain exporters that the EU was still ready to sell wheat abroad, after a surprise dip in its exports ruffled agricultural markets last week.

Guy Legras, director general of agriculture at the EU's Commission in Brussels, said he was satisified with recent sales of 300-400,000 tonnes a week. Last Thursday's drop to 70,000 tonnes was due to currency swings and attempts by exporters to secure excessive subsidies at a weekly tender, he said.

"We have given them (the private exporters) as much as they wanted. But last week we tightened the screw a bit because they were exaggerating. Their bids were not good last week," Legras said in a telephone interview.

Legras' projections have considerable influence over the grain trade, which sends in weekly applications to his department for subsidies to close the gap between EU prices and the lower prices importers are generally willing to pay.
The EU is the world's third largest wheat exporter behind the United States and Cannada.
Last week's decision to slow up exports frightened some investors who had sold short on Chicgao futures markets on Wednesday, prompting them to buy back contracts on Thursday.
Legras said the dollar's strength had also been a factor in the EU decision to close the throttle on exports for a while.

A stronger dollar -- now at its highest against the French franc, Europe's main domestic grain currency, since 1994 -- tends to make European wheat more competitive and therefore encourages the Commission to restrict subsidies to exporters.

The EU is seen as anxious to export wheat after landing a bumper crop of 90 million tonnes in 1996. So far this season it has exported around 6.5 million tonnes of bread wheat and may have up to another three million left to sell.
But Legras ruled out a more aggressive export stance, sought by some traders now that record Australian supplies are arriving on the world market and helping to drag down prices.
"We will never do it...The Australians are not on the same markets as us," he said.

Traders say that while the EU and Australia occasionally compete in some import markets like Egypt, the two do not generally fight for the same business. But any overall dip in prices caused by Australia's presence could force Brussels to increase the aid to its own exporters to help them keep up.
World wheat prices have fallen to around $150 a tonne from their peak of last April near $300, caused by low stocks. Analysts say prices continue to ease gradually.

Legras acknowledged that some wheat from last year's EU crop may not be exported at all, ending up in the EU's intervention storage system by the summer. But unlike some who warn of millions of tonnes being dumped in this way, Legras said he did not expect the amount of leftover wheat to be "gigantic".

The intervention system works by offering to buy in grain for EU stores at guaranteed floor prices if farmers cannot find a taker on the open market. The EU's silos have been practically empty for the past year in the wake of previous shortfalls.
